title: Ramayana's First Song 'Jai Jai Ram' Wins Fans, Praised For Visual Upgrades
excerpt: AR Rahman, Dr Kumar Vishwas, Arijit Singh, and Shreya Ghoshal's devotional track traces Ram and Sita's journey — and fans say the film's VFX has visibly improved since the teaser drew criticism.
body:
• Nitesh Tiwari's Ramayana released its first song, "Jai Jai Ram," on Monday, timed to Ganesh Chaturthi — the first extended musical look at Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi as Ram and Sita.
  • Composed by AR Rahman with lyrics by Dr Kumar Vishwas and vocals by Arijit Singh and Shreya Ghoshal, the devotional track traces the couple's journey from the Swayamvar to their return to Ayodhya.
  • Fans comparing the song's footage with earlier teasers praised visibly upgraded VFX and colour grading, with many saying the team appears to be acting on audience feedback.
  • Ramayana: Part 1 opens internationally on November 6, 2026, and in India on November 8 for Diwali; Part 2 follows at Diwali 2027.

The musical journey of Ramayana began Monday with "Jai Jai Ram," the first song from Nitesh Tiwari's two-part epic. Released on the occasion of Ganesh Chaturthi, hours after the makers dropped a new poster, the track offers the closest look yet at Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi as Lord Ram and Sita — and the internet responded within minutes.

The song brings together a heavyweight musical team: AR Rahman composed it, Dr Kumar Vishwas wrote the lyrics, and Arijit Singh and Shreya Ghoshal lend their voices. Rahman described the song's essence as the "simple and powerful repetition of Shri Ram's name," aiming to preserve the purity of a prayer while giving it cinematic scale. The orchestral score for the film also features contributions from Hans Zimmer, working alongside Rahman.

The music video follows Ram and Sita through the epic's defining chapters — the Swayamvar, their grand wedding, the journey into Vanavas, and the eventual return to Ayodhya — with tender, previously unseen moments between the couple. Fans seized on the chemistry between Kapoor and Pallavi, with one widely shared comment calling it devotion in its purest form: "Some songs are heard, some are felt. This one feels like devotion in its purest form." Another simply wrote, "Shreya and Arijit feels good."

Context & Background

Ramayana is structured as a two-part cinematic saga produced by Prime Focus Studios, DNEG, and Monster Mind Creations, and is reportedly one of the most expensive Indian films ever mounted, with a combined budget for both parts exceeding ₹4,000 crore. Tiwari, best known for Dangal and Chhichhore, has spent years developing the adaptation.

https://x.com/Adityakrsaha/status/2099482934919204948

The ensemble runs deep: Yash plays Ravana, Sunny Deol is Hanuman, and Ravi Dubey is Lakshman, with Vivek Oberoi as Vidyutjihva, Kajal Aggarwal as Mandodari, Rakul Preet Singh as Shurpanakha, and Lara Dutta as Kaikeyi. The trailer's release set new viewership benchmarks and generated worldwide buzz, but the early footage drew a split reaction — admiration alongside pointed criticism of the visual effects.

That criticism is what Monday's release quietly answered. Fans posted side-by-side "before and after" comparisons of scenes glimpsed in the trailer against the newer footage in the music video, praising the improved VFX and colour grading. The refrain across social media: the team is listening.

"We're listening closely, working diligently, and pouring every effort possible into honouring it with the reverence it holds."

— Namit Malhotra, producer, April 2026

Malhotra made those remarks in April, after the initial footage generated both praise and criticism online. He added that what audiences had seen at the time was "just the beginning" — a line Monday's release gave new weight to.

Impact & Analysis

Few films arrive with this kind of public visual-effects audit in progress. The pattern — release footage, absorb the internet's frame-by-frame critique, visibly upgrade before the next asset — is becoming standard for mega-budget Indian cinema, and Ramayana is now its most-watched case study. The strategy carries risk: it keeps the film's VFX under a microscope. But it also converts skeptics into stakeholders, and Monday's reaction suggests the conversion is working.

The Rahman-Zimmer pairing is the project's other headline. Zimmer's involvement alongside Rahman gives the film genuine Hollywood-scale scoring muscle, matched by a staggered global rollout: Australia on November 5, the international release on November 6, and India on November 8, timed to Diwali.

Diaspora Angle

Diaspora audiences get Part 1 first — the international release lands two days before the Indian one — and Diwali 2026 is already shaping up as a family event on overseas IMAX screens. For Indian communities abroad, a devotional track built around the Ram-Sita wedding arriving on Ganesh Chaturthi is about as well-timed a cultural signal as a film campaign can send.

What's Next

More singles are expected as the November rollout builds, with Part 1 hitting international theaters November 6 and India on November 8. The real test comes then: whether the visual polish fans are celebrating in a five-minute music video holds across a full-length epic — and whether Part 2, due Diwali 2027, can sustain the momentum.
